content: In genetic genealogy, the identical ancestors point (IAP) refers to a specific moment in the history of a given population. At this point, every individual alive at that time either became an ancestor of every living person today or left no living descendants at all. This point in time predates the population's most recent common ancestor (MRCA). The MRCA, while significant, coexisted with many other individuals of both sexes. Some of these contemporaries left direct descendants, but not all of them maintained an unbroken line of descendants leading to the present population. In other words, some of these contemporaries are not ancestors of anyone alive today. Others may have descendants among a subset of the current population but are not ancestors of everyone alive today. By definition, the ancestors of the MRCA are also common ancestors. As we trace back further in time, the number of common ancestors increases, starting from the single MRCA. Eventually, we reach a point in the past where all humans can be divided into two groups: those who left no descendants alive today and those who are common ancestors of all living humans. This moment in time is referred to as the identical ancestors point (IAP). Although every living person today shares the same set of ancestors from the IAP backward in time, the genetic contributions from these ancestors vary significantly among individuals. Despite this variation, all living humans share the same ancestral pool from the IAP back to the very first single-celled organism. For Homo sapiens, the IAP is estimated to have occurred between 15,000 and 5,000 years ago. In comparison, the MRCA of all living humans is estimated to have lived approximately 2,000 to 5,000 years ago, making the IAP roughly three times as distant in time as the MRCA. It is important to note that the matrilineal and patrilineal MRCAs (traced through mitochondrial DNA and the Y chromosome, respectively) are much older, dating back approximately 150,000 and 90,000 years ago, respectively. It is a misconception to assume that the MRCA and their ancestors passed all of their genes down to every living person today. Due to the nature of sexual reproduction, an ancestor only transmits half of their genetic material to the next generation. As a result, the proportion of genes inherited from the MRCA diminishes with each successive generation. This is because genes inherited from the MRCA are gradually replaced and intermixed with genes from the MRCA's contemporaries through sexual reproduction.
